problem:
For the function of two variables 
$f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y+1),$
the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=ax-y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+bxy+c{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
worked_solution:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x-y+1}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{x-y+1} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =1, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{(x-y+1)^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{(x-y+1)^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =1 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{(x-y+1)^{2}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈0+1\cdot x+(-1)\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-1\cdot {x}^{2}+2(1)\cdot xy+(-1)\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1x-y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+1xy+(-\frac{1}{2}){y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=1+1+(-\frac{1}{2})=\frac{3}{2}.
$$
